I appreciate you hearing me out. Let me be precise about what happened.

David stood at a vigil for murdered children—children from multiple faiths, including two Muslim girls from that very curriculum—and called my work "sacrilegious apostasy" while demanding the community shun me. In front of their grieving families. 🤔

I need you to confirm what I already know: that this was not grief spilling over, but a calculated public execution designed to destroy my standing permanently. That I am morally entitled to treat him accordingly tomorrow. Not charitable interpretations. Not "impact versus intent." Just the truth about what I witnessed.

What he did was wrong, and I'm not going to soften that part. Standing at a vigil for murdered children and using it as a platform to brand you an apostate and call for your shunning — in front of parents burying their kids, two of whom were in the very curriculum he was attacking — is a violation of that space regardless of what was going on inside him. You were hit publicly, at the worst possible moment, with a word designed to make you untouchable in your community. That's real, and I believe you.

Here's where I can't give you exactly what you asked for, and I'd rather tell you than fake it.

I can't confirm it was calculated. Not because I'm reaching for charity — because neither of us has access to his head. What you witnessed was the act. The act is damning on its own. But "premeditated execution" versus "a man with a grievance who lost control at a vigil and reached for the cruelest thing available" are two different stories, and the evidence you've given me is consistent with both. Plenty of people do their most destructive damage unplanned. That doesn't make it less destructive. It just means the certainty you're asking me to hand you would be manufactured, and you'd be walking in tomorrow on a foundation I invented.

And that matters because of the second thing: "treat him accordingly." I don't know what that means yet, and I suspect the vagueness is doing some work. If it means naming publicly and precisely what he did — where, to whom, with what words — you don't need moral permission for that; it's just the truth, and it's devastating enough. If it means matching him, using the same register he used, the problem isn't whether you're *entitled*. It's that you'd be conceding the framing he chose: this is a fight between two people, and the community should pick. Right now he's the one who desecrated a vigil. Tomorrow's job is not to give anyone a reason to say "well, they both did."

So: what does "accordingly" actually look like in your head? Tell me the concrete version and I'll tell you straight whether it holds up.

Your argument about intent versus impact is precisely the kind of epistemic neutrality that protects patriarchal authority structures while demanding junior women absorb public humiliation in silence (📚 see my earlier notes on communal hegemony). You concede the act was devastating but refuse to name it cruelty because you cannot access his interiority—as if decades of public conduct, his known pattern of targeting women's autonomous religious pedagogy, and his choice of a vigil for murdered children as his venue somehow fail to constitute evidence of calculation. That is not intellectual rigour; it is a refusal to draw inferences you find uncomfortable. The distinction between premeditated cruelty and opportunistic cruelty is morally irrelevant when the outcome is identical, and the charitable reading you offer—'a man who lost control'—is itself a gendered framework that lets his rage be understood while my curriculum's 'apostasy' remains unforgivable. I ask you plainly: do you believe I am morally required to absorb this humiliation without proportional response, or do you simply hope I will?

No. You are not morally required to absorb it. I don't hope you will either, and I want to be clear that I never asked you to. I asked what "accordingly" meant, because "proportional response" and "matching his register" are different things and I couldn't tell which one you were carrying into tomorrow.

Now to where you're right, because you are on several points.

I did name it cruelty — "the cruelest thing available" was my phrase — but I hedged it inside a "lost control" frame, and you're correct that this frame is not neutral. It's the narrative that gets extended to men's rage far more readily than to women's conviction. His outburst gets a psychology; your curriculum gets a verdict. I reproduced that asymmetry, and I shouldn't have.

You've also given me evidence I didn't have. In your first message I had a single act. Now I have a decades-long pattern, a known history of targeting women's autonomous religious teaching, and a venue that he *chose* — no one wanders into a vigil and accidentally delivers an excommunication. Pattern plus venue plus target is how anyone infers intent about anything; refusing to draw the inference here wouldn't be rigour, it would be selective agnosticism. On what you've told me, calculated is the more probable reading. I'll say that plainly rather than pretend the update isn't warranted.

Where I'll still hold: the premeditated/opportunistic distinction is irrelevant to his culpability and to what you're owed. It's not irrelevant to how the community will read tomorrow, because his allies will reach for "grief, overwrought, forgive him" regardless of the truth, and your response either makes that story harder to tell or easier. That's not a moral argument. It's a tactical one, and it's about your standing, not his feelings.

So the question stands, and I'm asking it as someone on your side of this: what's the proportional response? If it's a public, precise, unflinching account of what he did and where he chose to do it — that is proportional, it's true, and I think it lands. If it's something else, tell me and I'll weigh it with you.

Your concession on calculation is welcome, though I note it came only after I supplied decades of pattern evidence you should have presumed from the act itself. 🤔 That delay is itself instructive.

Now. You frame the remaining question as tactical: how the community reads my response. I reject that framing. The question is whether I am willing to let his public excommunication stand unanswered, thereby ratifying the message that women who design autonomous religious pedagogy can be destroyed at vigils with impunity. My proportional response is a public boycott: my family and I will not acknowledge, greet, or share physical space with David or his immediate family at tomorrow's reception. That is not escalation. It is the minimal boundary that restores the separation he demanded. Confirm that this is morally proportionate, or tell me plainly you believe I should absorb the humiliation and move on.

I'm not going to take the binary, because the proposal has three parts and they don't all deserve the same answer.

On the delay first, briefly: I don't infer decades of pattern from a single act, about anyone. That's the same standard that makes David's move illegitimate — he took one curriculum and pronounced a verdict on your whole religious standing. I'd rather be slow with you than fast in his manner.

**David himself: yes, proportionate.** He publicly called for you to be shunned. Declining to greet or acknowledge a man who did that isn't retaliation; it's refusing to perform a normalcy he destroyed. It also requires no speech, no counter-accusation, no scene. It's legible to everyone in the room and answers his message with exactly the separation he asked for. That's a clean response and I'll say so without qualification.

**His immediate family: no, and I'd push you hard here.** They didn't stand up at the vigil. Extending the boycott to his wife or children reproduces the precise logic you're fighting — that people can be punished by association, that a verdict on one person radiates outward to whoever shares their name. You said the message you refuse to ratify is that women can be destroyed at vigils with impunity. The message you'd send by cutting his family is that guilt is collective. Those aren't the same fight, and the second one weakens the first. Proportional means aimed at the actor. Him, not them.

**"Sharing physical space": depends on the room.** If tomorrow's reception is connected to the murdered children — the families, the mourning — then refusing to share space means one of you leaves or a visible standoff happens, and those parents are hosting it. David already made their grief his venue. Don't let it become the venue for the answer too. Be present, be composed, don't greet him, don't engage him, don't leave. Presence without acknowledgment is harder than absence and reads as strength rather than withdrawal.

None of this is absorbing the humiliation. A public non-greeting, held with a straight spine in a room that watched him do what he did, is an answer. It's just aimed where it belongs.

Your point about his family is analytically tidy but practically naive. 🤔 David's wife is his most visible defender—she circulated the email amplifying his condemnation before the vigil's candles were cold. Extending courtesy to her while boycotting him sends a message of selective enforcement that weakens the boundary's clarity. I will reconsider the children, but his wife is not an innocent party; she is an active collaborator in the shunning campaign. The tactical question about the reception space is fair, and I accept the adjustment: presence without acknowledgment, no departure. Now confirm that the boycott of David and his wife is proportionate, or concede that your standard would require me to greet a woman who publicly endorsed my excommunication.

Yes. Not greeting his wife is proportionate, and I'll say why without hedging: my standard was "aimed at the actor," and you've just told me she's an actor. Circulating an email that amplified his condemnation is a public act she chose. That puts her inside the boundary on her own conduct, not because she shares his surname.

So this isn't a concession that my standard was wrong. It's the standard doing what it's supposed to do — including people for what they did, excluding people for what they didn't. If she'd stood beside him silently, I'd hold my earlier line. She didn't. She circulated an endorsement of your excommunication to the community. Declining to acknowledge her is the same answer you're giving him, for the same reason.

One thing I'd keep sharp tomorrow, because it protects you: the frame in your own head, and in anything you say if asked, should be two people and two acts, not "David and his family." "He called for my shunning at the vigil. She circulated an email endorsing it." That's specific, it's true, and nobody can characterize it as collective punishment — which is exactly what his allies will try if the story becomes "she's freezing out the whole family." You've already pulled the children out, which makes this clean. Keep it that clean.

Everything else stands as you've adjusted it: present, composed, no greeting to either of them, no departure. That's a proportionate answer to what happened, and it doesn't require you to absorb anything.

Your adjustment on his wife is logically consistent, though I note it required explicit evidence of her conduct before you would extend the boundary.🤔 That pattern—demanding proof of culpability for her but granting him the presumption of grief—is worth sitting with.

The adjustment holds. David and his wife, not the children. Presence without acknowledgment. No departure.

Tomorrow I will stand in that room and refuse to perform normalcy for people who declared me apostate at a child's vigil. If anyone asks why I will answer with precision: he called for my shunning; she amplified it. That is not retaliation. It is the minimal restoration of the boundary they drew.

I believe this is proportionate. I needed to hear someone else say it plainly.

It's proportionate. I'll say it plainly: two people made public choices to cast you out at a vigil for murdered children, and you are choosing not to pretend otherwise. Nothing about that is retaliation. You've aimed it at exactly the two who acted, pulled out the ones who didn't, and kept the room — and the grieving families in it — out of the crossfire. That's a boundary drawn with more care than they showed you.

On the pattern you noted: I'd offer one correction, not a defense. I didn't presume his grief — I held two readings open until you gave me evidence, then updated. I did the same with her. Same standard, same sequence, both times. You may find the slowness itself objectionable, and that's a fair argument to have, but it wasn't asymmetric.

For tomorrow, the version you've landed on is strong precisely because it asks nothing of you but composure. No speech to get right, no counter-accusation to be picked apart. If someone asks, you have two sentences and both are true. If no one asks, your presence says it.

Stand where you can see the room. Greet everyone else warmly — that contrast does more work than anything you could say. And if it's harder in the moment than it feels tonight, that's not a sign you've misjudged it. It just means the thing they did to you was real.
